problem: Drops the detail of the wooden steps 'the "boots" placed for my convenience' as she descends.
new_text: Reader, though I look comfortably settled, my mind is far from calm. I expected someone to meet me when the coach stopped here. I looked around anxiously as I stepped down the wooden steps the inn's boot-boy had set out for me, expecting to hear my name called and to see a carriage waiting to take me to Thornfield. There was nothing. When I asked a waiter if anyone had inquired for a Miss Eyre, the answer was no. So I had no choice but to ask for a private room, and here I sit waiting, while all kinds of doubts and fears trouble my thoughts.

problem: 'Negus' (hot wine with water and sugar) rendered as 'hot toddy' (a spirit drink); changes what is served.
new_text: "Oh, it's no trouble. I'm sure your hands are nearly frozen. Leah, make a little hot spiced wine and cut a sandwich or two. Here are the keys to the storeroom."

problem: Drops 'having taken the key from the lock' — Mrs. Fairfax takes the hall-door key upstairs with her.
new_text: I thanked her for the thoughtful choice, and since I truly was worn out from the journey, I said I was ready to go up. She took her candle, and I followed her out of the room. First she checked that the front door was locked and, taking the key from the lock, led me upstairs. The steps and banisters were oak. The staircase window was tall and latticed. Both the window and the long gallery where the bedroom doors opened looked as though they belonged in a church rather than a house. A cold, vault-like air filled the stairs and gallery, creating a bleak sense of space and solitude. I was glad, when finally shown into my room, to find it small and furnished in a plain, modern style.

problem: 'would not at least recoil from me with antipathy' is intensified to 'shrink from me in horror', exaggerating Jane's modest hope.
new_text: I got up and dressed with care. I was obliged to dress plainly—every article of clothing I owned was made with extreme simplicity—but I was by nature careful about my appearance. It wasn't my habit to be careless about how I looked or the impression I made. On the contrary, I always wanted to look as well as I could, and to please as much as my lack of beauty would allow. I sometimes regretted that I wasn't prettier. I sometimes wished for rosy cheeks, a straight nose, and a small, shapely mouth. I wished I were tall, stately, and well-proportioned. I felt it was a misfortune to be so small, so pale, and to have such irregular, striking features. And why did I have these wishes and regrets? It would be hard to say—I couldn't clearly explain it to myself at the time, though I had a reason, a logical, natural one. In any case, once I had brushed my hair very smooth and put on my black dress—which, Quaker-like as it was, at least had the virtue of fitting perfectly—and straightened my clean white collar, I thought I would look respectable enough for Mrs. Fairfax, and that my new pupil wouldn't at least recoil from me in dislike. Having opened my window and checked that everything on the dressing table was neat and tidy, I ventured out.

problem: Adèle's French loses its accent: source 'C'est là ma gouvernante!' appears as 'C'est la', which is incorrect French.
new_text: "C'est là ma gouvernante!" she said, pointing at me and speaking to her nurse, who answered—

problem: Proper-noun diacritic dropped: source 'Madame Frédéric' appears twice as 'Madame Frederic'.
new_text: "With Madame Frédéric and her husband. She looked after me, but she's no relation. I think she's poor, because her house wasn't as nice as Mama's. I wasn't there long. Mr. Rochester asked if I'd like to go and live with him in England, and I said yes, because I knew Mr. Rochester from before I knew Madame Frédéric, and he was always kind to me and gave me pretty dresses and toys. But he hasn't kept his word—he brought me to England and then went away again, and I never see him."

problem: Source 'when the morning had advanced to noon' is changed to 'when mid-morning came', changing the timing (the laugh scene later happens at 'high noon').
new_text: I found my pupil cooperative enough, though reluctant to concentrate. She hadn't been accustomed to any kind of regular work. I felt it would be unwise to push her too hard at first. So after talking to her a great deal and getting her to learn a little, when the morning had worn on to noon I let her go back to her nurse. I then planned to spend the time before dinner making some sketches for her to use.

problem: 'one vast window' becomes 'one magnificent window', dropping its size.
new_text: As I was going upstairs to fetch my portfolio and pencils, Mrs. Fairfax called to me. "Your morning lessons are finished now, I suppose?" She was in a room whose folding doors stood open. I stepped in when she spoke. It was a large, stately room with purple chairs and curtains, a Turkish carpet, walnut-paneled walls, one vast window rich in stained glass, and a high, beautifully molded ceiling. Mrs. Fairfax was dusting some vases of fine purple stone that stood on a sideboard.

problem: 'like types of the Hebrew ark' is reduced to 'miniature arks', losing the biblical allusion (the Ark of the Covenant); 'a home of the past' becomes 'a museum of the past'.
new_text: When we left the dining room, she offered to show me the rest of the house. I followed her up and down, admiring everything. It was all well arranged and handsome. The large front bedrooms struck me as especially grand. And some of the third-floor rooms, though dark and low-ceilinged, were fascinating in their antiquity. Furniture once used in the main rooms had been moved up here as fashions changed. In the dim light coming through narrow windows, I saw bedsteads a hundred years old, oak and walnut chests carved with palm branches and cherubs' heads that looked like copies of the Hebrew Ark, rows of venerable high-backed chairs, and even older stools whose cushions still showed traces of half-faded embroidery, worked by hands that had been dust for two generations. These relics gave the third floor of Thornfield Hall the feel of a home of the past—a shrine of memory. I liked the hush, the gloom, the quaintness of these rooms in daylight. But I certainly didn't want to sleep in one of those wide, heavy beds—some enclosed behind oak doors, others curtained with ancient English tapestries crusted with thick needlework depicting strange flowers, even stranger birds, and the strangest human figures. All of which would have looked eerie indeed in pale moonlight.

problem: Drops that the path through the wood was 'visibly overgrown'.
new_text: "Up to the roof—would you like to come and see the view?" I followed her up a very narrow staircase to the attics, then up a ladder and through a trapdoor to the roof. I was now level with the rooks' colony and could peer into their nests. Leaning over the battlements and looking far down, I surveyed the grounds spread out like a map: the bright, velvety lawn closely circling the gray base of the house; the park-like field dotted with ancient trees; the woods, brown and dry, divided by a path, clearly overgrown, that was greener with moss than the trees were with leaves; the church at the gates; the road; the peaceful hills—all basking in the autumn sunshine. The horizon was bounded by a clear sky, blue marbled with pearly white. Nothing in the scene was extraordinary, but everything was lovely. When I turned away and went back through the trapdoor, I could barely see my way down the ladder. The attic seemed pitch-black compared to the arch of blue sky I'd been gazing at, and the sunlit scene of grove, meadow, and green hills over which the hall presided.

problem: Certainty raised: source 'perhaps Grace Poole' becomes 'Probably Grace Poole'.
new_text: "One of the servants, most likely," she answered. "Perhaps Grace Poole."

problem: Source 'as tragic, as preternatural a laugh' loses 'tragic', which Jane uses for the laugh.
new_text: I truly hadn't expected anyone called Grace to appear, because the laugh had been as tragic and as unnatural as any I'd ever heard. If it hadn't been broad noon, with nothing ghostly about the circumstances—if neither the place nor the time encouraged fear—I would have been superstitious enough to be frightened. But what happened next showed me I was foolish to feel even surprise.

problem: Source 'a woman of between thirty and forty' becomes a precise 'about thirty-five'.
new_text: The nearest door opened and a servant came out—a woman of between thirty and forty, with a stocky, square build, red hair, and a hard, plain face. A less romantic or less ghostly apparition could hardly be imagined.

problem: Diacritic dropped in Adèle's French: source 'vous êtes servies' appears as 'vous etes'.
new_text: "Mesdames, vous êtes servies!" adding, "J'ai bien faim, moi!"

problem: Adèle's French farewell 'Revenez bientôt, ma bonne amie, ma chère Mdlle. Jeannette' is replaced by an English translation. Elsewhere (11.61–62, 11.79, 11.123, chs. 13–14) the edition keeps her French unglossed, and here the context (a goodbye answered with a kiss) makes the meaning clear.
new_text: October, November, and December passed. One afternoon in January, Mrs. Fairfax had requested a holiday for Adèle because she had a cold. Since Adèle backed the request with an enthusiasm that reminded me how precious holidays had been in my own childhood, I agreed, thinking it right to be flexible. It was a fine, calm day, though very cold. I was tired of sitting still in the library all morning. Mrs. Fairfax had just written a letter that needed posting, so I put on my bonnet and cloak and volunteered to carry it to Hay—a pleasant two-mile walk on a winter afternoon. After settling Adèle comfortably in her little chair by Mrs. Fairfax's fire, giving her the best wax doll (which I usually kept wrapped in silver paper in a drawer) and a storybook for variety, and answering her "Revenez bientôt, ma bonne amie, ma chère Mdlle. Jeannette" with a kiss, I set out.

problem: 'to enjoy and analyse the species of pleasure' loses 'analyse', part of Jane's self-observing voice.
new_text: The ground was hard, the air was still, the road was deserted. I walked fast until I was warm, then slowed to enjoy and analyze the particular pleasure the hour and the setting offered me. It was three o'clock. The church bell tolled as I passed beneath the tower. The charm of the hour lay in the approaching dusk, in the low, pale sun sliding down the sky. I was a mile from Thornfield, in a lane known for wild roses in summer, for nuts and blackberries in autumn, and even now adorned with a few bright red hips and haws. But its greatest winter beauty was its total solitude and bare stillness. If any breeze stirred, it made no sound here—there was no holly, no evergreen to rustle. The stripped hawthorn and hazel bushes were as motionless as the white, worn stones that paved the middle of the path. On either side, far and wide, there were only fields with no grazing cattle, and the small brown birds that occasionally stirred in the hedge looked like single russet leaves that had forgotten to fall.

problem: Misapplied qualifier: in the source the soft 'ripplings and whisperings' are 'at once so far away and so clear'. The modern text makes the noise itself break in 'suddenly, clearly'.
new_text: A harsh noise broke through these delicate ripplings and whisperings, at once so far away and so clear: a definite tramp, tramp, a metallic clattering that drowned out the soft whispering, the way a solid crag or the rough trunk of a great oak in the foreground of a painting blots out the pale distance of blue hills, sunlit horizon, and melting clouds.

problem: Drops Jane's self-deprecating 'amongst other rubbish' about her memories of nursery stories.
new_text: The noise was on the path: a horse was approaching. The bends of the lane still hid it, but it was coming closer. I was just leaving the stile, but since the path was narrow, I sat back down to let it pass. In those days I was young, and all kinds of bright and dark fancies filled my mind. Among the other rubbish there were memories of nursery tales, and now that I was older, they had a force and vividness that childhood could never have given them. As this horse drew near and I watched for it to appear through the dusk, I remembered certain of Bessie's stories featuring a North of England spirit called a Gytrash—which, in the form of a horse, mule, or large dog, haunted lonely roads and sometimes appeared to travelers caught out after dark, as this horse was now appearing to me.

problem: Drops 'beaver' from 'a black beaver bonnet'.
new_text: "You're not a servant at the hall, obviously. You are—" He stopped, running his eye over my clothes, which as usual were plain: a black wool cloak, a black beaver bonnet—neither half fine enough for a lady's maid. He seemed puzzled about what I was. I helped him.

problem: The quotation marks around the allusion 'too easy chair' are dropped, so it no longer reads as a quotation.
new_text: I didn't want to go back inside Thornfield. To cross its threshold was to return to stagnation. To pass through the silent hall, climb the dark staircase, find my lonely little room, and then sit with tranquil Mrs. Fairfax through the long winter evening—hers the only company—was to completely extinguish the faint excitement my walk had kindled. To slip back into the invisible chains of a routine too still and too unchanging—a life whose very privileges of safety and ease I was becoming unable to appreciate. What good it would have done me then to be tossed in the storms of an uncertain, struggling life, to learn from rough and bitter experience to long for the calm I now found stifling! Yes—exactly as much good as it does a man tired of sitting still in a "too easy chair" to take a long walk. And the wish to move was just as natural in my circumstances as it would be in his.
